## How old is the electricity in your lamp?

Most people guess minutes, or hours, as if electricity waited in a warehouse until someone needed it. Almost always, the answer is less than a second. The grid stores very little. So at every moment, power plants must make as much electricity as everyone is using: no more, no less.

Someone has to keep that balance. In Prairie Town, a small town on the Great Plains, that someone is you. Your shift lasts 24 hours.
:::

```{=html}

<li data-value="less">None: the town will have to use less</li>

</section>
```

## Play: run Prairie Town for a day {#play}

```{=html}
<p>In the interactive, you step through the 24 hours of one spring day. Each hour shows the town's demand and what the nuclear plant (a flat 100 MW), the wind farm and the solar farm produce. You set the combined-cycle gas plant and the gas peaker, and a gauge shows the grid frequency: 60 Hz when supply equals demand, lower when power is short, higher when there is too much. Tallies add up the running cost, the CO₂ and the energy served, unserved and spilled. The figure above shows the day as a simple expert rule runs it: wind and solar fill much of the morning and midday, the combined-cycle plant follows the rest, and the peaker helps in the evening, when demand peaks and the sun has set.</p>
```

## What just happened

```{=html}
<div class="lx-reveal" data-reveal="g0-evening" data-answer="gas">
<p class="lx-kicker">Your prediction</p>
<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>
<p><strong>The gas plants.</strong> The nuclear plant runs flat, so it cannot follow the evening rise. Wind and solar give only what the weather gives, and the sun is gone. Only the gas plants can be turned up on request. At the evening peak, even the combined-cycle plant at full power is not enough, so the peaker runs too.</p>
</details>
</div>
```

### Balancing: supply must equal demand {#balancing}

Electricity is used the moment it is made. If the plants make less than people use, the big spinning generators slow down a little, and the grid's frequency drops below 60 hertz (60 cycles per second). If they make more, the generators speed up and the frequency rises. North American grids are designed to stay in a very narrow band around 60 Hz ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/todayinenergy/detail.php?id=3990)). That is why your gauge reads hertz: frequency is the grid's balance meter. If it falls too far, protective equipment disconnects some customers so that the rest of the grid survives. In the game, that is *unserved* energy.

### Power and energy {#power-and-energy}

Your sliders set **power**, in megawatts (MW): how fast a plant makes electricity right now. The tallies count **energy**, in megawatt-hours (MWh): how much was made over time. One equation links them:

::: {.lx-equation}
energy (MWh) = power (MW) × time (hours)
:::

A plant running at 50 MW for one hour makes 50 MWh. Each step of the game is one hour, so every MW you set becomes that many MWh in the tallies. Lesson 1 is all about this difference.

### Dispatchable and variable plants {#dispatchable-and-variable}

The gas plants are **dispatchable**: the operator can order them up or down. Wind and solar are **variable**: they make what the weather gives. The operator can turn them down (this is called spilling, or *curtailing*, their output) but cannot turn them up.

The nuclear plant ran flat. Real nuclear plants can change their output, but most run near full power almost all the time: in 2025, U.S. nuclear plants averaged 91% of their full output over the year ([EIA](https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/nuclear/us-nuclear-industry.php)).

Gas plants differ in speed. Your combined-cycle plant could change by only 40 MW an hour. Real combined-cycle plants change faster once they are running, but starting one from cold can take hours; the game's limit stands in for that. The peaker can jump to any level, which makes it useful in the evening rush.

### Cheapest first {#cheapest-first}

The expert's rule uses the plants in order of running cost: wind and solar first (they burn no fuel), then nuclear (cheap fuel, and here it runs anyway), then the combined-cycle plant, and the peaker last. This order is called the **merit order**. Two mistakes cost money: running the peaker when the cheaper gas plant could do the job, and burning gas while free wind is spilled. The second also adds CO₂ for nothing.

The rule is simple, and it does not plan ahead. In the evening its slow gas plant falls behind and the peaker fills in. If you warm up the combined-cycle plant an hour or two early, you can beat it.

### What the game leaves out {#simplifications}

- **Prairie Town is an island.** It cannot buy power from its neighbours. Real grids connect plants and towns across thousands of miles.
- **The forecast is perfect.** Real operators plan with forecasts that miss (lesson 4).
- **The game moves in one-hour steps.** Real grids balance second by second (lesson 3).
- **Nothing breaks.** Plants never fail, and the power lines never fill up.
- **The gauge's scale is made up.** In the game, each MW out of balance moves the frequency by 0.01 Hz.

```{=html}
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="lx-deeper-k">Go deeper · Analyst</span><span class="lx-deeper-t">The balance, energy and cost as equations</span></summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

For every hour $t$, let $p_g(t)$ be the output of plant $g$ in MW (for wind and solar, what the weather allows), $u(t)$ the unserved demand, $s(t)$ the spilled power and $d(t)$ the demand. Then

$$\sum_g p_g(t) + u(t) - s(t) = d(t).$$

Energy, cost and CO₂ are sums over the hours, with $\Delta t = 1$ hour, a running cost $c_g$ in \$/MWh and an emission rate $e_g$ in t/MWh:

$$E_g = \sum_t p_g(t)\,\Delta t, \qquad C = \sum_t \sum_g c_g\,p_g(t)\,\Delta t, \qquad \mathrm{CO_2} = \sum_t \sum_g e_g\,p_g(t)\,\Delta t.$$

Check it against the expert's day: 2,400 MWh of nuclear, 1,510 MWh from the combined-cycle plant and 90 MWh from the peaker give $C = 2400 \times 10 + 1510 \times 40 + 90 \times 100 = \$93{,}400$ and $1510 \times 0.37 + 90 \times 0.55 = 608.2$ t of CO₂.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="lx-deeper-k">Go deeper · Modeler</span><span class="lx-deeper-t">The operator's job as a small optimization problem</span></summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The decisions are the gas outputs $p_\mathrm{cc}(t)$ and $p_\mathrm{pk}(t)$, the spilled power $s(t)$ and the unserved demand $u(t)$, for each of the 24 hours. With $w(t)$ and $v(t)$ the available wind and solar output and $V$ a large penalty for unserved energy:

$$\min \; \sum_{t} \big( 40\,p_\mathrm{cc}(t) + 100\,p_\mathrm{pk}(t) + V\,u(t) \big)$$

subject to, for every hour $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
100 + w(t) + v(t) + p_\mathrm{cc}(t) + p_\mathrm{pk}(t) + u(t) - s(t) &= d(t) && \text{(balance)}\\
0 \le p_\mathrm{cc}(t) \le 200, \qquad 0 \le p_\mathrm{pk}(t) &\le 100 && \text{(plant sizes)}\\
-40 \le p_\mathrm{cc}(t) - p_\mathrm{cc}(t-1) &\le 40 && \text{(ramp limit)}\\
0 \le s(t) \le w(t) + v(t), \qquad u(t) &\ge 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The nuclear plant's cost is the same in every plan, so it drops out. Every term is linear, so this is a *linear program*. The expert's rule solves it one hour at a time, without looking ahead. Solving all 24 hours together warms up the combined-cycle plant before the evening climb. On this day that saves \$1,300, about 1.4% of the running cost, and cuts the peaker's energy from 90 to 65 MWh. Can you find that plan by hand?

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<p class="lx-modnote"><i class="bi bi-diagram-3" aria-hidden="true"></i><span><strong>Modeler's note.</strong> The decisions, goal and rules in your end-of-day summary are the three parts of every optimization model. Lesson 10, <a href="index.html#lesson-10">Write it down</a>, turns them into symbols. Lesson 11, <a href="index.html#lesson-11">Ask the solver</a>, gives this problem to a real solver and shows how to check its answer. Both are upcoming.</span></p>
```
:::

::: {.lx-check #check}
## Check yourself

```{=html}
<div class="lx-quiz lx-myths" data-quiz="g0-myth">
<p class="lx-kicker">Myth or fact?</p>
<div class="lx-cards">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="store" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">“A power plant can store electricity for later.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="myth">Myth<span class="lx-why">Plants make electricity at the moment it is used. Storing it takes a separate device, such as a battery. Prairie Town has none, which is why spilled wind is simply lost.</span></li>
<li data-value="fact">Fact<span class="lx-why">It sounds plausible, but plants make electricity at the moment it is used. Storing it takes a separate device, such as a battery.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Plants make electricity at the moment it is used; storing it takes a separate device, such as a battery.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="freq" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">“If supply is greater than demand, the grid's frequency rises.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="myth">Myth<span class="lx-why">It is a fact. Extra power speeds up the spinning generators, so the frequency climbs above 60 Hz. Too little power does the opposite.</span></li>
<li data-value="fact">Fact<span class="lx-why">Extra power speeds up the spinning generators, so the frequency climbs above 60 Hz. Too little power does the opposite.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Extra power speeds up the spinning generators, so the frequency climbs above 60 Hz.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="wind" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">“A wind farm can be told to make more power when demand rises.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="myth">Myth<span class="lx-why">Operators can turn a wind farm down, but not up beyond what the wind allows. That is what <em>variable</em> means.</span></li>
<li data-value="fact">Fact<span class="lx-why">Operators can turn a wind farm down, but not up beyond what the wind allows. That is what <em>variable</em> means.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A wind farm can be turned down, but not up beyond what the wind allows.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="g0">
<p class="lx-kicker">Quick questions</p>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="gap" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext"><span class="lx-qnum">1</span>At 7 p.m., demand is 367 MW. Nuclear makes 100 MW, wind 42 MW and solar nothing. How much must the two gas plants make together?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="a">367 MW<span class="lx-why">That would double the supply. Gas only fills the gap that the other plants leave: 367 − 100 − 42 = 225 MW.</span></li>
<li data-value="b">225 MW<span class="lx-why">367 − 100 − 42 − 0 = 225 MW. That is more than the combined-cycle plant's 200 MW, so the peaker must help.</span></li>
<li data-value="c">267 MW<span class="lx-why">That leaves out the wind. Subtract every plant that is already running: 367 − 100 − 42 = 225 MW.</span></li>
<li data-value="d">325 MW<span class="lx-why">That leaves out the nuclear plant's 100 MW: 367 − 100 − 42 = 225 MW.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>225 MW: 367 − 100 − 42 − 0. That is more than the combined-cycle plant's 200 MW, so the peaker must help.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="energy" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext"><span class="lx-qnum">2</span>The peaker runs at 50 MW for 3 hours. How much energy does it make?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="a">50 MWh<span class="lx-why">That is one hour's worth. Energy adds up over time: 50 MW × 3 h = 150 MWh.</span></li>
<li data-value="b">150 MWh<span class="lx-why">Energy = power × time = 50 MW × 3 h = 150 MWh.</span></li>
<li data-value="c">150 MW<span class="lx-why">The number is right, the unit is not. MW is power, a rate. An amount of energy is in MWh.</span></li>
<li data-value="d">53 MWh<span class="lx-why">Power and time multiply; they do not add. 50 MW × 3 h = 150 MWh.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>150 MWh: energy = power × time = 50 MW × 3 h.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="spill" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext"><span class="lx-qnum">3</span>On a sunny afternoon, nuclear, wind and solar already make more than the town needs. Your combined-cycle plant is still at 40 MW. What happens?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices">
<li data-value="a">The lights go out<span class="lx-why">No: there is too much power, not too little.</span></li>
<li data-value="b">More wind and solar is spilled, and you pay for gas nobody needed<span class="lx-why">The grid stays balanced by spilling wind and solar, so you pay for gas and emit CO₂ for nothing. Turn gas down when the sun is strong.</span></li>
<li data-value="c">The extra power is saved for the evening<span class="lx-why">Prairie Town has no storage. Power that is not used at once is lost.</span></li>
<li data-value="d">The frequency falls below 60 Hz<span class="lx-why">Too much power would push the frequency up, not down. Here the grid spills wind and solar instead, so it stays at 60 Hz.</span></li>
</ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>More wind and solar is spilled, and you pay for gas (and emit CO₂) for nothing.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.lx-real #real-world}
## In the real world

Each hour of your day had its own mix of plants, so each hour's electricity carried a different amount of CO₂: the evening hours, when gas ran hardest, were the dirtiest. Real grids work the same way, and the data are public. The U.S. Energy Information Administration's [Hourly Electric Grid Monitor](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/) shows demand and generation by fuel for each balancing authority, hour by hour. In my [study of carbon-aware electricity use](../projects/ghg.qmd), I used these hourly data to ask how much the emissions attributed to electricity use fall when consumption moves toward cleaner hours. The answer was modest: moving load helps, but the gain is limited by how much load can move and by how much the grid's mix changes over a day.
:::
